topic: pressing apples for cider and coaxing a slow ferment through the winter

provenance.author: glowny-en-a
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is load-and-cask arithmetic on the same pressing with closed task questions, base is a diagnosis of falling juice yields and a sluggish ferment. Grounded external referent: the press, introduced in turn 0 and carried through the whole diagnosis (its blinded cloths and jumping screw are the fault, and the clean juice it gives explains the slow start).

a: Here are five loads of apples for the tally, and their crate counts need adding in order.
The first load has fourteen crates and the second load has eleven crates on the slip.
The third has nine crates, and the fourth has eight crates from the same orchard row.
The fifth load is the smallest of the group at six crates on the trailer.
How many crates do the five loads come to when every slip is added together?
base: Our pressing days give barely half the juice they did when my father ran them.
We mill the apples to pulp, wrap it in cloths, and stack the layers under the screw.
The press is the old rack and cloth kind, and it has stood in the barn for decades.
This season a full load of pulp gave ninety litres where we once drew one hundred forty.
What should we look at first before the late apples come in from the orchard?

a: Added in order, the running counts are fourteen, then twenty-five, then thirty-four crates so far.
The last two entries bring the count to forty-two and then forty-eight crates in all.
At twenty kilograms to each full crate, the first load weighs two hundred eighty kilograms.
The second load then weighs two hundred twenty kilograms at that same twenty kilogram rate.
Does the crate total of forty-eight match the number chalked on the barn door slate?
base: A drop that size rarely comes from the fruit alone, so start with the pulp itself.
Coarse pulp sheds far less juice, and a worn mill will leave hard chunks in every layer.
Old cloths blind over with dried pomace too, and blinded cloth lets almost nothing through.
Watch the press on the next load and see whether juice stops early or never runs hard.
Does the screw still pull down smoothly, or does it jump and stick as you turn it?

a: Now work out the juice for each load at six litres from every ten kilograms.
List the juice for all five loads in the first to fifth order given above.
Round every figure to the nearest whole litre before it goes onto the page.
Send the two biggest loads to the long trough and the other three to the short one.
Which juice figure belongs to the third load at that fixed rate of six litres?
base: The screw jumps near full pressure, and juice stops running long before the layers look spent.
The press cloths are the same set we have used for at least six or seven autumns.
When we break the stack apart, the middle layers come out wet and heavy with juice.
The mill blades have never been changed, and the pulp does carry hard slices of apple.
Would new cloths and sharper blades bring the yield back on their own this season?

a: The first load gives one hundred sixty-eight litres of juice at the stated rate.
The second gives one hundred thirty-two litres, and the third gives one hundred eight.
The fourth load gives ninety-six litres, and the fifth and smallest load gives seventy-two litres.
The long trough therefore takes three hundred litres of juice from its two loads together.
The short trough takes two hundred seventy-six litres from the three smaller loads put together.
base: Wet middle layers confirm it, since juice from the centre must travel through every blinded cloth.
New cloths will give you the biggest single gain, and they cost less than lost juice.
Have the mill blades sharpened as well, and aim for pulp like coarse wet breadcrumbs.
Build thinner layers, eight of them rather than five, so the juice has shorter paths out.
Then take the press up to pressure slowly, over an hour, letting it rest between turns.

a: One correction before we carry on: the fourth load holds nine crates, not eight.
Recalculate its weight and its juice, and leave the other four loads exactly as they stand.
Then give the new totals for crates and for litres across all five loads together.
After that, list the loads in the order their juice goes into casks this week.
Which load goes in first under the order second, then first, then fifth, then third?
base: New cloths arrived on Tuesday and the blades came back from the grinder the same week.
The next load ran one hundred thirty litres, which is close to the old full measure.
Now the juice sits in casks in the barn, and it has barely begun to work.
After ten days there is only a whisper of froth on the top of each cask.
Should a fresh cask be bubbling hard by the second week of standing there?

a: With nine crates the fourth load weighs one hundred eighty kilograms on the same rate.
Its juice becomes one hundred eight litres, and the crate total rises to forty-nine.
The new juice total across the five loads is five hundred eighty-eight litres exactly.
The filling order stands as second, then first, then fifth, then third, then fourth last.
The second load therefore fills first, and the fourth load closes the filling this week.
base: A whisper after ten days means the yeast is cold, not gone, so do not panic yet.
Juice straight off a cold autumn pressing can lie still for weeks in an unheated barn.
The press gave you clean juice this time, and clean juice starts slower than murky runnings.
Move one cask somewhere that holds fifteen degrees and watch it against the ones left cold.
If the warm cask wakes within a week, warmth is the whole story this year.

a: Convert the five hundred eighty-eight litres into casks that hold one hundred ten litres each.
Tell me how many full casks that fills and what remains for the part cask.
Then split the remainder into two even jugs and give the figure for each one.
The filling starts at nine in the morning with casks done forty minutes apart.
How many full casks does five hundred eighty-eight litres come to at that size?
base: We moved one cask beside the kitchen wall where the chimney keeps the corner mild.
Within five days its lock was ticking steadily while the barn casks stayed nearly silent.
There is room in that corner for three casks at most if we shift the dresser.
The other five casks would have to stay out in the cold barn regardless.
Is a slow cold ferment in the barn actually worse than the quick warm one indoors?

a: Five hundred eighty-eight litres fills five full casks with thirty-eight litres left over.
Each of the two jugs takes nineteen litres when the remainder splits evenly between them.
The first cask is done at nine forty and the second at ten twenty.
The third is done at eleven, the fourth at eleven forty, the fifth at twelve twenty.
The part cask follows at one, closing a filling day of four hours in all.
base: Slow and cold is not worse, and many makers would call it the better road.
A long cool ferment keeps the sharp apple smell that a fast one boils away.
The barn casks may run into spring, and they will need topping up as they go.
Keep the locks wet, keep the casks full, and let the cold ones take their time.
Move the kitchen casks back out once they quiet down, so the whole set ages together.

a: Write out a four step cellar sheet for the crew in the order set down here.
Step one is filling, step two is fitting locks, step three is labelling every cask.
Step four is stacking, and each step needs its clock time written on the sheet.
Filling begins at nine in the morning and stacking must finish by four in the afternoon.
Fitting locks takes thirty minutes and labelling takes twenty minutes for the whole set.
base: We will keep three casks by the chimney and leave the other five to their slow road.
My son has started a pressing book with a page for every load and every cask.
Each page carries the pulp weight, the litres drawn and the day the lock first ticked.
The new cloths get rinsed and dried after every pressing day and stored on the beam.
Next autumn we will sharpen the blades before the season instead of halfway through it.

a: Step one runs from nine until one, covering the five casks and the part cask.
Step two runs from one until half past one, taking the thirty minutes allowed.
Step three runs from half past one until ten to two for the whole set.
Step four runs from ten to two until three, leaving an hour of slack in hand.
The cellar sheet then closes with all six casks stacked and labelled before four.
base: That book will be worth more than any single fix you made this year.
Rack every cask off its thick sediment once the first hard working has died down.
Taste monthly through spring, and bottle when the sharpness has softened into something round.
Keep back a few bottles from the first good cask as a marker for later seasons.
By next autumn the pages will tell you what a full load ought to give, week by week.
